edges.description: Loss of tyrosine aminotransferase activity prevents normal tyrosine degradation, causing tyrosine to accumulate in blood and tissues.
Elevated intracellular tyrosine deposits in the cornea and in palmoplantar epidermis, triggering the inflammatory and hyperkeratotic tissue response.
Sustained untreated hypertyrosinemia is associated with variable cognitive manifestations through unresolved neurologic intermediates.
Hypertyrosinemia is associated with reported seizures through unresolved neurologic intermediates.
Hypertyrosinemia is associated with reported self-injurious behavior through unresolved neurologic intermediates.
Corneal tyrosine deposition drives an inflammatory pseudodendritic keratitis.
Corneal crystal deposition produces the characteristic corneal dystrophy and opacity.
Epidermal tyrosine deposition in the palms and soles produces painful focal hyperkeratosis.

nodes.description: Lifelong low-protein diet restricting dietary tyrosine and phenylalanine, combined with phenylalanine-free/tyrosine-free amino acid, vitamin, and mineral supplements. Lowering plasma tyrosine produces rapid resolution of the corneal and cutaneous lesions. Early-treated individuals may be asymptomatic or have only mild ocular and skin manifestations.

evidence.reference_title: Point mutations in the tyrosine aminotransferase gene in tyrosinemia type II.
evidence.snippet: The disease results from deficiency in hepatic tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT; L-tyrosine:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase, EC 2.6.1.5), a 454-amino acid protein encoded by a gene with 12 exons.
